lead: A signal defined on an interval behaves like a vector: every instant of time is one component. Two tools carry over from vector algebra. The inner product measures how much two signals resemble each other, and the norm measures a signal's size, which here is its energy. When the inner product is zero the signals are orthogonal, and a complete orthogonal set acts as a coordinate system. Each coefficient is a single inner product, and Parseval's relation rebuilds the total energy from those coefficients. Fourier series, QAM and OFDM modems, and image compression all rest on this picture.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for signal notation and Chapter 1.2 for the energy of a signal.

sections.h3: Inner product: similarity as one number

blocks.text: A vector v = (v₁, v₂, …, v_N) has N components, and its dot product with another vector is a sum of component-by-component products. A signal has one component for every instant of time. Replace the sum by an integral and the dot product becomes the inner product.

blocks.where: a and b are the interval limits, in seconds; y*(t) is the complex conjugate of y(t), obtained by flipping the sign of its imaginary part; for real signals y*(t) = y(t).
the sum runs over the sample indices in the chosen range; n is the integer sample index; this is the discrete-time version.

blocks.text: The inner product is a single number. A large value means the two signals rise and fall together on that interval; a value near zero means they share no common pattern there.

blocks.where: ‖x‖ is the norm of x; |x(t)|² is the squared magnitude; ‖x‖² is exactly the energy of x on [a, b], so the norm is the square root of energy.

blocks.text: The distance between two signals is ‖x − y‖, the square root of the energy of the error signal. Two signals are orthogonal when ⟨x, y⟩ = 0.

items: ⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨y, x⟩* and ⟨x, x⟩ is real and never negative.
The inner product is linear in its first slot: ⟨ax₁ + bx₂, y⟩ = a⟨x₁, y⟩ + b⟨x₂, y⟩.
⟨x, x⟩ = 0 only for a signal that is zero almost everywhere.

sections.h3: Orthogonal sets and the coefficient formula

blocks.text: A set of signals φ₁, φ₂, … is orthogonal on an interval when ⟨φ_m, φ_n⟩ = 0 for every m ≠ n. It is orthonormal when each signal also has unit norm, ‖φ_n‖ = 1; then ⟨φ_m, φ_n⟩ = δ_mn, which equals 1 when m = n and 0 otherwise.

Orthogonality is what makes coefficients easy. Write x = Σ_n c_n φ_n and take the inner product of both sides with φ_m. Every term with n ≠ m gives zero, so one term survives and the coefficient falls out.

blocks.where: c_n is the coefficient of φ_n in the expansion of x; the numerator is one inner product; the denominator is the energy of that basis signal. For an orthonormal set the denominator is 1 and c_n = ⟨x, φ_n⟩.

items: Fix the interval; orthogonality is meaningless without it.
Check the set is orthogonal on that interval.
Compute each ‖φ_n‖² by integrating the squared basis signal.
Divide to get c_n, then sum Σ c_n φ_n to rebuild x.

blocks.text: A complete set leaves nothing behind: no nonzero signal is orthogonal to every φ_n. With a complete set the sum Σ c_n φ_n reproduces x in energy, and the residual x − Σ c_n φ_n has zero norm. With an incomplete set the residual is a genuine signal, orthogonal to the whole set, that the basis simply cannot describe.
Energy is the inner product of a signal with itself. Substitute the expansion and expand: the cross terms ⟨φ_m, φ_n⟩ with m ≠ n all vanish, leaving only the diagonal terms.

blocks.where: the left side is the total energy of x on [a, b]; |c_n|²‖φ_n‖² is the energy carried by the n-th component; the discrete-time form replaces the integral by Σ |x[n]|².

blocks.text: So the energy splits cleanly among the basis signals, with no cross-energy terms. Each coefficient squared, times the energy of its basis signal, is that component's share. This is the same statement as Pythagoras' theorem in a right triangle.

Engineers read power per band from Parseval: the share of energy in each Fourier harmonic, or the power in each subcarrier of an OFDM symbol, comes straight from the coefficients instead of a fresh integral.

figure.caption: A signal and any orthogonal set feed the inner products; dividing by ‖φ_n‖² gives the coefficients, which rebuild the signal and give its energy through Parseval.

spec.title: Signal space
spec.aria: A signal and an orthogonal basis set feed inner products, which produce coefficients for reconstruction and for Parseval energy.

examples.question: On the interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, take φ₁(t) = 1 and φ₂(t) = 2t − 1. (a) Show they are orthogonal. (b) Find ‖φ₁‖² and ‖φ₂‖². (c) For x(t) = 3φ₁(t) + 4φ₂(t), find the energy using Parseval, and verify by direct integration.
steps: (a) ⟨φ₁, φ₂⟩ = ∫₀¹ 1·(2t − 1) dt = [t² − t]₀¹ = (1 − 1) − (0 − 0) = 0. Nonzero signals with zero inner product, so they are orthogonal on [0, 1].
(c) Since x is already written in the basis, c₁ = 3 and c₂ = 4. Parseval: energy = c₁²‖φ₁‖² + c₂²‖φ₂‖² = 9(1) + 16(1/3) = 9 + 16/3 = 43/3 ≈ 14.33.
Check directly: x(t) = 3 + 4(2t − 1) = 8t − 1, so ∫₀¹ (8t − 1)² dt = ∫₀¹ (64t² − 16t + 1) dt = 64/3 − 8 + 1 = 64/3 − 7 = 43/3. Both routes agree.
examples.answer: φ₁ and φ₂ are orthogonal on [0, 1]; ‖φ₂‖² = 1/3; the energy of x(t) = 3φ₁ + 4φ₂ is 43/3 ≈ 14.33 energy units.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction as F
ip = F(0, 1)
n1sq = F(1, 1)
n2sq = F(1, 3)
energy = 9 * n1sq + 16 * n2sq
print(float(ip))
print(float(n1sq))
print(float(n2sq))
print(float(energy))

traps: Orthogonality depends on the interval. φ₁(t) = 1 and φ₂(t) = 2t − 1 give inner product 0 on [0, 1] but ∫₀²(2t − 1)dt = 2 on [0, 2], so they are not orthogonal there.
For complex signals use the conjugate: ⟨x, y⟩ = ∫x(t)y*(t)dt, not ∫x(t)y(t)dt. Dropping the star gives a different number and can make a self inner product complex.
Divide by ‖φ_n‖² whenever the set is not orthonormal. In the worked example ‖φ₂‖² = 1/3, so a coefficient computed as ⟨x, φ₂⟩ alone is 3 times too small.
Orthogonality is a property of a pair of signals on an interval, not of one signal alone; a single function is never 'orthogonal' without a partner.
Zero energy means the zero signal, not a zero inner product: ⟨x, y⟩ = 0 does not imply x = 0 or y = 0.

quiz.q: Define orthogonal signals on an interval.
quiz.a: x and y are orthogonal on [a, b] when ⟨x, y⟩ = ∫ₐᵇ x(t)y*(t)dt = 0. The discrete-time form uses Σ x[n]y*[n].

quiz.q: State Parseval's relation for an orthogonal set {φ_n} on an interval.
quiz.a: ∫|x(t)|²dt = Σ |c_n|²‖φ_n‖², with c_n = ⟨x, φ_n⟩/‖φ_n‖². The total energy equals the sum of the component energies.

quiz.q: Why does the coefficient formula divide by ‖φ_n‖² rather than by ‖φ_n‖?
quiz.a: Taking ⟨x, φ_m⟩ with x = Σc_nφ_n leaves c_m⟨φ_m, φ_m⟩ = c_m‖φ_m‖². Energy appears squared, so the division is by ‖φ_m‖². If the set is orthonormal, ‖φ_m‖² = 1 and no division is visible.

quiz.q: What does it mean for an orthogonal set to be complete, and what is lost if it is not?
quiz.a: No nonzero signal is orthogonal to every φ_n. Then x − Σc_nφ_n has zero norm and the expansion reproduces x exactly in energy. An incomplete set leaves a nonzero residual, orthogonal to the whole set, that the basis cannot represent.

quiz.q: On 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, take φ₁(t) = 1 and x(t) = t. Find c₁ and the energy carried by c₁φ₁.
quiz.a: ‖φ₁‖² = 1. ⟨x, φ₁⟩ = ∫₀¹ t dt = 1/2. So c₁ = (1/2)/1 = 1/2, and the component energy is c₁²‖φ₁‖² = 1/4 = 0.25, less than the total energy 1/3 ≈ 0.333.

quiz.q: An orthonormal basis gives coefficients c₁ = 2, c₂ = −1, c₃ = 2. Find the energy of x on the interval.
φ₁(t) = 1 and φ₂(t) = 2t − 1 are orthogonal on [0, 1]. Compute their inner product on [0, 2] and explain what this means for a coefficient computed on that interval.
quiz.a: ∫₀²(2t − 1)dt = [t² − t]₀² = 4 − 2 = 2 ≠ 0, so the pair is not orthogonal on [0, 2]. The cross term no longer vanishes: ⟨x, φ₁⟩ then contains a contribution from c₂⟨φ₂, φ₁⟩, so c₁ = ⟨x, φ₁⟩/‖φ₁‖² is not the correct coefficient for this basis on this interval.

beyond: Not for the exam. In an OFDM modem the subcarriers are made orthogonal over one symbol period, so each subcarrier's data is recovered by one inner product at the receiver. QAM constellations are points in a two-dimensional signal space built from two orthonormal waveforms. Compressed sensing goes further and asks how few inner products are needed to recover a sparse signal. Wavelets replace the single sinusoid basis with scaled and shifted versions that stay orthogonal, which is why JPEG 2000 works. Search for 'signal space representation', 'Gram–Schmidt for signals' and 'orthogonal frequency division multiplexing' to go deeper.
